faq.a: Yes; early ischaemic changes may be invisible. Clinical syndrome and later imaging confirm the diagnosis.
faq.q: Can a patient with normal CT still have an MCA stroke?

faq.a: Aspirin is cheap, widely available, and has proven benefit; clopidogrel is reserved for aspirin‑intolerant patients.
faq.q: Why is aspirin preferred over clopidogrel in most MCA strokes?

faq.a: Expressive or receptive aphasia accompanying unilateral weakness.
faq.q: What bedside sign suggests a dominant‑hemisphere MCA stroke?

exam: What immediate investigations would you order for a patient with sudden right‑sided weakness and speech difficulty? — CT head to exclude bleed, glucose, and if possible CTA to assess for large‑vessel occlusion.

A 58‑year‑old with rheumatic mitral stenosis presents with left MCA syndrome. Which secondary‑prevention drug is indicated and why? — Anticoagulation (warfarin) because the stroke is cardio‑embolic from atrial fibrillation or left atrial thrombus.
How does the NIHSS help you decide on thrombolysis? — Scores ≤15 generally meet eligibility; higher scores indicate severe stroke but do not automatically exclude treatment if imaging is favourable.

A patient cannot get a CT scan within 4 hours. What alternative management can you provide? — Start aspirin promptly, control blood pressure, and arrange transfer to a centre with imaging; consider bedside transcranial Doppler if available.
What clinical feature distinguishes an MCA infarct from a lacunar stroke? — Presence of cortical signs such as aphasia, visual field loss, or neglect, which are absent in lacunar strokes.
Why is alteplase contraindicated in a patient with recent major surgery? — The risk of severe bleeding outweighs benefit; recent surgery is a major bleed risk factor.
Explain why aggressive fluid resuscitation is avoided in malignant MCA infarction. — Excess fluids increase cerebral oedema and raise intracranial pressure, worsening herniation risk.
What rehabilitation goal is most important in the first week after an MCA stroke? — Prevent complications (e.g., DVT, pressure sores) and begin early mobilisation to improve functional outcome.
ai.title: Middle Cerebral Artery Stroke
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Acute middle cerebral artery (MCA) stroke is the most common large‑vessel brain infarct, causing contralateral face‑arm‑leg weakness and language deficits when dominant. Prompt recognition, imaging, and targeted management are vital, especially where resources are limited.

b: Ischaemic: CT/CTA shows hypodensity or vessel occlusion without bleed.
Haemorrhagic: CT shows hyperdense clot within MCA territory.
sections.p: An MCA stroke is a sudden loss of blood flow to the territory supplied by the middle cerebral artery, either by thrombosis, embolism, or haemorrhage. Diagnosis rests on clinical syndrome and imaging.

b: NIHSS 0‑4: minor, 5‑15: moderate, >15: severe.
ASPECTS 10‑0: higher scores = less early infarct; ≤7 predicts poor outcome.
sections.p: Severity is graded by the NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) and by imaging (ASPECTS) for early ischaemic changes.

b: Cardio‑embolic: atrial fibrillation, rheumatic heart disease, prosthetic valves.
Atherosclerotic plaque rupture in internal carotid or MCA.
Infectious: HIV vasculitis, TB meningitis, malaria‑related cerebral vasospasm.
sections.p: In low‑resource settings the leading causes are cardio‑embolic (e.g., rheumatic mitral stenosis, atrial fibrillation), large‑artery atherosclerosis, and infectious vasculitis (e.g., HIV‑related, TB meningitis).

b: Face, arm, leg weakness – greater in arm than leg.
Contralateral sensory loss.
Aphasia (dominant) or neglect (non‑dominant).
Homonymous visual field defect (contralateral).
sections.p: Rapid onset (seconds‑minutes) of unilateral weakness, sensory loss, and cortical signs. Dominant‑hemisphere strokes add aphasia; non‑dominant add neglect.

t.b: Is the stroke haemorrhagic? – Hyperdensity = bleed; normal/low density = ischaemia.
Is there a large‑vessel occlusion? – Shows clot location; guides thrombectomy.
Is hypoglycaemia mimicking stroke? – <70 mg/dL suggests metabolic cause.
Is infection or inflammation contributing? – Elevated ESR/CRP may point to TB/HIV vasculitis.
Is a cardio‑embolic source present? – A‑fib or valvular disease detected.

t.a: If CT unavailable, bedside transcranial Doppler
t.b: Can detect large‑vessel flow reduction; useful when imaging delayed.

b: Rapid neurological decline – suggests haemorrhagic conversion.
Brain oedema causing herniation – decreasing consciousness, pupil changes.
Seizures – new focal motor activity.
Deep vein thrombosis – immobilisation.
sections.p: Complications develop quickly and raise mortality.

b: If within 4.5 h and no bleed: give IV alteplase (if available) – dissolves clot.
If large‑vessel occlusion and endovascular service: mechanical thrombectomy up to 24 h.
Antiplatelet (aspirin) for non‑cardio‑embolic ischaemia – reduces recurrence.
Anticoagulation (warfarin/DOAC) for cardio‑embolic source – prevents further emboli.
Control blood pressure (target <185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis).
Manage glucose, temperature, and treat seizures if present.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, protect the penumbra, and prevent complications.

b: Statin therapy for all atherosclerotic strokes.
Lifestyle: smoking cessation, diet low in salt/fats, regular exercise.
Screen for atrial fibrillation – consider long‑term anticoagulation.
Physiotherapy, speech therapy, and occupational therapy for functional recovery.
sections.p: Secondary prevention focuses on risk‑factor modification and rehabilitation.

b: Lacunar infarct – small deep infarcts causing pure motor or sensory loss, not cortical signs.
Posterior circulation stroke – vertigo, ataxia, cranial nerve deficits rather than face‑arm‑leg weakness.
Seizure with post‑ictal paresis (Todd’s paralysis) – resolves within hours.
Early CT may appear normal in ischaemia – do not rule out stroke if clinical picture fits.
Hyperglycaemia can mask neurological deficits – treat glucose first.
Mild elevation of ESR/CRP may be due to infection unrelated to stroke.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of consciousness, worsening weakness, new seizures, or signs of brain herniation (e.g., unequal pupils).
